summary: Satellites have tracked active fire since 2000, but the record is split between MODIS (2000–) and VIIRS (2012–), and their detections can’t be compared directly. Over the same Australian fires, VIIRS reports 15.7 times as many fire pixels as MODIS, and stitching the two records naively invents a +187% jump in burning in 2012 that never happened. Emberline harmonizes them into one consistent record and turns it into a burning-activity calendar for any area a user draws. It converts every NASA FIRMS hotspot into daily burning presence on a shared grid, removes industrial heat sources, and calibrates VIIRS to MODIS region by region over the years both satellites flew. For any area it shows the typical fire season, percentile bands, the critical period, weeks running outside historical norms, a 1–4 week outlook, and a calendar export. I tested it on 2.5 million real NASA detections over New South Wales from 2000 to 2026: held-out years were predicted within 3.6% (naive stitching: 153%), and the 2019 Black Summer is correctly flagged as a record high. Emberline gives responders, scientists and land managers a consistent picture of when and where burning happens.
details:
What it does - Emberline turns 26 years of NASA satellite fire detections into a burning-activity calendar for any area. Draw a box or polygon, or pick a preset, and it shows that area’s typical fire season (the weeks holding 80% of activity), its critical period (50%), the peak week, and percentile bands for every week. It flags weeks and whole seasons running outside historical norms, gives a 1–4 week outlook with its measured skill, and exports the season as a calendar file for Google Calendar or Outlook.

How it works - (1) Every MODIS and VIIRS detection from NASA FIRMS becomes daily burning presence on a shared 0.25° grid, binned by local solar day, so pixel counts never cross the sensor boundary. (2) Industrial heat sources such as steelworks, refineries and gas flares are removed using FIRMS type flags plus a persistence filter. (3) A model calibrates VIIRS to MODIS region by region over 2012–2019, using pixel count, fire radiative power, night share and neighbouring activity. (4) Only one VIIRS satellite (S-NPP) carries the record, so the NOAA-20 and NOAA-21 launches and MODIS orbit drift don’t distort the trend.

Validation on real data - On 2.5 million detections over New South Wales (2000–2026), held-out years were predicted within 3.6% on average, against 153% for naive stitching. Spatial accuracy is r = 0.956, against 0.907 for a simple ratio. The industrial-heat filter found 92% of NASA’s own static-source labels without seeing them. On five-satellite data over Australia, held-out weeks came within 6.4%, against 174% naive.

Impact - Emergency responders get critical periods and early-warning anomaly flags. Scientists get trends that reflect the fire, not the satellite. Land managers get a weekly picture of when burning peaks. One real finding: across much of NSW, satellite-detected burning peaks in autumn (planned hazard-reduction and stubble burns), while summer wildfire dominates only in extreme years.

Tools - Python (pandas, NumPy, SciPy, scikit-learn), FastAPI, NASA FIRMS API, Leaflet, D3.js, three.js (WebGL globe), GitHub Pages and GitHub Actions. 33 automated tests.

Creativity and factors considered - I validated against real held-out data, not just a demo. The live demo mode walks judges through the app and hands them the mouse. I disclose limits honestly: the outlook’s skill is small and shown as measured, and separating planned burns from wildfire needs land-cover data I haven’t added yet.
